title: The Strangest House Anyone Ever Lived In
paragraphs: Nobody could have imagined a sweeter or more mysterious place. The high walls around it were covered with the bare stems of climbing roses, so thick that they were matted together. Mary Lennox knew they were roses because she had seen so many of them in India. The ground was all wintry brown grass, and clumps of bushes grew out of it that were surely rosebushes, if they were alive. There were plenty of standard roses whose branches had spread so wide that they looked like little trees. There were other trees in the garden too. One of the things that made the place look so strange and lovely was that climbing roses had run all over them and let long tendrils hang down, making light, swaying curtains. Here and there the tendrils had caught hold of one another, or of a far-reaching branch, and crept from one tree to the next, making lovely bridges. There were no leaves or roses on them now, and Mary did not know whether they were dead or alive. But their thin gray or brown branches and sprays looked like a hazy cloak spread over everything: the walls, the trees, and even the brown grass. In places the tendrils had fallen from their supports and run along the ground. This hazy tangle from tree to tree was what made it all look so mysterious. Mary thought it must be different from other gardens, because it had been left all alone for so long. And it truly was different from any other place she had ever seen in her life.
“How still it is!” she whispered. “How still!”

Then she waited a moment and listened to the stillness. The robin had flown up to his treetop, and he was as still as everything else. He did not even flutter his wings. He sat without moving and looked at Mary.
“No wonder it’s still,” she whispered again. “I’m the first person to speak in here for ten years.”

Stepping as softly as if she were afraid to wake someone, she moved away from the door. She was glad of the grass under her feet, because it kept her footsteps silent. She passed beneath one of the fairy-like gray arches between the trees and gazed up at the sprays and tendrils that made it.
“I wonder if they’re all completely dead,” she said. “Is it a completely dead garden? I wish it weren’t.”

If she had been Ben Weatherstaff, she could have told by looking at the wood whether it was alive. But all she could see was gray and brown sprays and branches, and not one of them showed even a tiny leaf-bud anywhere.
Still, she was _inside_ the wonderful garden. Any time she liked, she could come back through the door under the ivy, and it felt as though she had found a whole world of her own.

The sun was shining inside the four walls. The high arch of blue sky over this one corner of Misselthwaite seemed even brighter and softer than it did over the moor. The robin flew down from his treetop and hopped about, or flew after her from one bush to the next. He chirped a great deal and looked very busy, as if he were showing her things. Everything was strange and silent, and she seemed to be hundreds of miles from anyone. Somehow she did not feel lonely at all. The only thing that troubled her was wanting to know whether all the roses were dead. Perhaps some had lived, and would put out leaves and buds as the weather got warmer. She did not want it to be a completely dead garden. If it were truly alive, how wonderful it would be, and what thousands of roses would grow on every side!

Her skipping rope had been hanging over her arm when she came in. After she had walked about for a while, she decided to skip all the way around the garden, stopping whenever she wanted to look at something. There seemed to have been grass paths here and there. In one or two corners there were alcoves of evergreen with stone seats, or tall flower urns covered in moss.

Near the second of these alcoves she stopped skipping. A flowerbed had once been planted there, and she thought she could see something poking up out of the black soil—sharp little points, pale green in color. Ben Weatherstaff’s words came back to her, and she dropped to her knees to examine them.
“Yes, they’re tiny growing things. They _could_ be crocuses, or snowdrops, or daffodils,” she whispered.
Leaning in close, she breathed in the fresh smell of the damp soil. It pleased her very much.
“Maybe there are others coming up in other places,” she said. “I’ll go all over the garden and look.”

She did not skip. She walked. She went slowly and kept her eyes on the ground. She looked in the old flower beds and among the grass. After she had gone all the way around, trying not to miss anything, she had found ever so many more sharp, pale green points. She had become quite excited again.
“It’s not a completely dead garden!” she cried softly to herself. “Even if the roses are dead, other things are alive.”

She did not know anything about gardening. But in some of the places where the green points were pushing through, the grass was so thick that they didn’t seem to have room to grow. She searched around until she found a fairly sharp piece of wood. Then she knelt down and dug, and pulled out the weeds and grass until she had made nice little clear spaces around them.

“Now they look as if they can breathe,” she said when she had finished the first ones. “I’m going to do ever so many more. I’ll do every one I can see. If I don’t have time today, I can come back tomorrow.”

She went from place to place, digging and weeding. She enjoyed herself so much that she was led on from bed to bed and into the grass under the trees. The work made her so warm that she took off her coat first, and then her hat. All the while, without knowing it, she was smiling down at the grass and the pale green points.

The robin was tremendously busy. He was very pleased to see gardening begun on his own land. He had often wondered about Ben Weatherstaff. Where there is gardening, all sorts of delicious things to eat get turned up with the soil. Now here was a new kind of creature, not half Ben’s size, who had been clever enough to come into his garden and start right away.

Mistress Mary kept working in her garden until it was time for her midday dinner. She was actually a little late remembering it. As she put on her coat and hat and picked up her skipping rope, she could hardly believe two or three hours had gone by. All that time she had been truly happy. Dozens and dozens of tiny pale green points now showed in the cleared spots, and they looked twice as cheerful as they had when grass and weeds were smothering them.
“I’ll come back this afternoon,” she said, looking all around at her new kingdom and speaking to the trees and rosebushes as if they could hear her.

Then she ran lightly across the grass, pushed open the slow old door, and slipped through it under the ivy. Her cheeks were so red, her eyes so bright, and she ate such a dinner that Martha was delighted.
“Two pieces o’ meat and two helpings o’ rice pudding!” she said. “Eh! Mother will be pleased when I tell her what the skipping rope’s done for you.”

While she was digging with her pointed stick, Mistress Mary had come across a sort of white root, rather like an onion. She had put it back in its place and patted the earth carefully down over it. Now she wondered if Martha could tell her what it was.
“Martha,” she said, “what are those white roots that look like onions?”

“They’re bulbs,” answered Martha. “Lots o’ spring flowers grow from ’em. The very little ones are snowdrops and crocuses, and the big ones are narcissuses and jonquils and daffydowndillys. The biggest of all are lilies and purple flags. Eh! They’re lovely. Dickon’s got a whole lot of ’em planted in our bit o’ garden.”
“Does Dickon know all about them?” Mary asked, struck by a new idea.
“Our Dickon could make a flower sprout from a brick path. Mother says he simply whispers things up out o’ the ground.”
“Do bulbs last a long time? If nobody looked after them, would they live for years and years?” Mary asked anxiously.

“They look after themselves,” said Martha. “That’s why poor folk can afford ’em. Leave ’em alone, and most of ’em’ll work away underground their whole lives, spreading out and having little ’uns. There’s a spot in the park woods here with snowdrops by the thousands. When spring comes, it’s the prettiest sight in Yorkshire. Nobody knows when they were first planted.”
“I wish it were spring right now,” said Mary. “I want to see everything that grows in England.”
She had finished her dinner and gone to her favorite seat on the hearth rug.
“I wish—I wish I had a little spade,” she said.
“Whatever do you want a spade for?” asked Martha, laughing. “Are you going to take up digging? I’ll have to tell Mother that, too.”

Mary watched the fire and thought it over. If she meant to keep her secret kingdom, she had to be careful. She wasn’t doing any harm. But if Mr. Craven discovered the open door, he would be terribly angry. He would get a new key and lock the garden up for good, and she simply could not bear that.

“It’s such a big, lonely place,” she said slowly, as though she were working things out as she spoke. “The house is lonely, and so are the park and the gardens. So many places are shut up. I never did much in India, but there was more to look at—natives, and soldiers marching past, and sometimes a band playing—and my Ayah told me stories. Here there’s nobody to talk to except you and Ben Weatherstaff. You have your work to do, and Ben Weatherstaff hardly ever speaks to me. I was thinking that with a little spade I could dig somewhere, the way he does. Maybe I could make a little garden, if he’d give me some seeds.”
Martha’s face lit up.

“There now!” she exclaimed. “If that isn’t one o’ the things Mother said! She says, ‘There’s such a lot o’ room in that big place. Why don’t they give her a bit for herself, even if she plants nothing but parsley and radishes? She’d dig and rake and be right down happy over it.’ Those were the very words she said.”
“Did she?” said Mary. “She knows so many things, doesn’t she?”
“Eh!” said Martha. “It’s like she says: ‘A woman who brings up twelve children learns something besides her A B C. Children are as good as arithmetic for setting you finding things out.’”
“How much would a spade cost—a little one?” Mary asked.

“Well,” Martha answered thoughtfully, “there’s a shop or two in Thwaite village, and I saw little garden sets there. A spade, a rake and a fork, all tied together, for two shillings. And they looked sturdy enough for real work.”
“I have more than that in my purse,” said Mary. “Mrs. Morrison gave me five shillings, and Mrs. Medlock passed on some money from Mr. Craven.”
“Did he remember you that much?” exclaimed Martha.
“Mrs. Medlock told me I could have a shilling a week for spending. She hands me one every Saturday. Until now I couldn’t think what to spend it on.”

“My word! That’s riches,” said Martha. “You can buy anything in the world you want. The rent on our cottage is only one and threepence, and it’s like pulling teeth to get it. Now I’ve just thought of something,” she said, putting her hands on her hips.
“What?” said Mary eagerly.

“The shop at Thwaite sells packets o’ flower seeds, a penny each, and our Dickon knows which ones are prettiest and how to get ’em growing. Many a day he walks over to Thwaite just for the fun of it. Can you print letters?” she asked suddenly.
“I know how to write,” Mary answered.
Martha shook her head.
“Our Dickon can only read printing. If you could print, we could write him a letter and ask him to go and buy the garden tools and the seeds at the same time.”
“Oh, you’re a good one!” Mary cried. “You really are! I never knew you were so kind. I’m sure I can print if I try hard. Let’s ask Mrs. Medlock if we can borrow pen, ink and paper.”
“I’ve some o’ my own,” said Martha. “I bought it so I could print a little letter to Mother on Sundays. I’ll run and fetch it.”
Martha hurried out of the room. Mary stood by the fire, twisting her thin little hands together in pure delight.
“With a spade,” she whispered, “I could make the ground soft and nice and dig out the weeds. And if I have seeds and can get flowers growing, the garden won’t be dead at all—it will come to life.”

She did not go out again that afternoon. When Martha came back with her pen and ink and paper, she had to clear the table and carry the plates and dishes downstairs. When she got to the kitchen, Mrs. Medlock was there and told her to do something. So Mary waited what seemed to her a very long time before Martha returned. Then writing to Dickon turned out to be a serious piece of work. Mary had been taught very little, because her governesses had disliked her too much to stay with her. She couldn’t spell especially well, but she found that she could print letters when she tried. This was the letter Martha dictated to her:
“_My Dear Dickon:_

I hope this letter finds you well, as it leaves me at present. Miss Mary has plenty of money. Would you go to Thwaite and buy her some flower seeds, and a set of garden tools for making a flower bed? Choose the prettiest seeds, and ones that are easy to grow, since she has never done this before and comes from India, which is a different sort of place. Give my love to Mother and all of you. Miss Mary is going to tell me a lot more, so on my next day out you can hear about elephants and camels, and gentlemen who go hunting lions and tigers.
“Your loving sister,
“Martha Phœbe Sowerby.”
“We’ll slip the money into the envelope, and I’ll have the butcher boy carry it in his cart. He’s a great friend o’ Dickon’s,” Martha said.
“How will I get the things when Dickon buys them?”
“He’ll bring ’em to you himself. He’ll like to walk over this way.”
“Oh!” exclaimed Mary. “Then I’ll see him! I never thought I would see Dickon.”
“Do you want to see him?” asked Martha suddenly, because Mary looked so pleased.
“Yes, I do. I’ve never met a boy that foxes and crows love. I want very much to meet him.”
Martha gave a little start, as if she had remembered something.
“Now, to think,” she broke out, “to think o’ me forgetting that! And I thought I was going to tell you first thing this morning. I asked Mother—and she said she’d ask Mrs. Medlock her own self.”
“Do you mean—” Mary began.
“What I told you on Tuesday. Ask if you could be driven over to our cottage one day, to have a bit o’ Mother’s hot oat cake with butter, and a glass o’ milk.”
All the interesting things seemed to be happening in a single day. Imagine going across the moor in broad daylight, with a blue sky overhead! Imagine stepping into a cottage full of twelve children!
“Does she think Mrs. Medlock would let me go?” she asked, quite anxiously.
“Aye, she reckons so. She knows Mother’s a tidy woman, and how spotless she keeps our cottage.”
“If I went, I’d meet your mother as well as Dickon,” said Mary. She turned the idea over and liked it very much. “She doesn’t sound like the mothers in India.”

Mary’s work in the garden and the excitement of the afternoon left her feeling calm and thoughtful. Martha stayed until teatime, and the two of them sat in easy quiet, hardly talking at all. But just as Martha was about to go downstairs for the tea tray, Mary asked her a question.
“Martha,” she said, “has the scullery maid had the toothache again today?”
Martha certainly started a little.
“What makes you ask that?” she said.

“I waited a long time for you to come back, so I opened the door and walked down the corridor to see if you were coming. And I heard that faraway crying again, just like the other night. There isn’t any wind today, so you can see it couldn’t have been the wind.”
“Eh!” said Martha, fidgeting. “You mustn’t go walking about in corridors and listening. Mr. Craven would be so angry there’s no telling what he’d do.”
“I wasn’t listening,” said Mary. “I was only waiting for you, and I heard it. That’s three times now.”
“My word! That’s Mrs. Medlock’s bell,” said Martha, and she nearly ran out of the room.

“It’s the strangest house anyone ever lived in,” said Mary sleepily, as she let her head sink onto the cushioned seat of the armchair beside her. The fresh air, the digging and the skipping-rope had made her so pleasantly tired that she fell asleep.
